Alexander Hamilton. Alexander Hamilton was a Founding Father of the United States whose bold financial and political vision shaped the young nation's economic system and constitutional structure. A self-made immigrant from the Caribbean, he rose from poverty to become George Washington's trusted aide, a delegate to the Constitutional Convention, the chief architect of American financial policy as the first Secretary of the Treasury, and one of the three principal authors of the Federalist Papers. His rivalry with Thomas Jefferson defined American politics in the seventeen nineties, and his legacy remains divisive, celebrated as the creator of American economic power and condemned for his monarchist sympathies.

Born in the British West Indies in seventeen fifty-seven, or seventeen fifty-five with records unclear, illegitimate and orphaned, he educated himself and emigrated to New York as a teenager, working his way up through hard work and writing. He served as George Washington's aide-de-camp during the Revolutionary War, forming a deep bond with Washington and absorbing military and political leadership firsthand.

Hamilton drafted The Federalist essays with Madison and Jay between seventeen eighty-seven and eighty-eight to argue for ratification of the U.S. Constitution, providing the most authoritative commentary on constitutional intent and design. These essays remain the definitive guide to understanding the founders' thinking. At the Constitutional Convention, he proposed the notion of a powerful executive, noting in his notes a president for life though this was later tempered, and a bicameral legislature, sketching the framework for a strong central government.

As Secretary of the Treasury from seventeen eighty-nine to ninety-five under Washington, he established the nation's financial credibility by assuming state war debts into federal debt, creating a national bank, and establishing a federal mint, building the institutional foundation of American capitalism. He advocated for tariffs to protect American manufacturing, the creation of a merchant marine, and federal investment in infrastructure, laying out a proto-industrial vision that later Republicans would embrace.

He clashed repeatedly with Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson over the scope of executive power and the role of commercial interests in government, a rivalry that crystallized into nascent Democratic-Republican and Federalist parties.
